lessons.title: A Plan for Your Money
lessons.objective: Explain a plan for your money and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A budget assigns money to needs, saving, and things you value.
Plan using money actually available rather than hoped-for income.
Choosing one use leaves less for another, which is an opportunity cost.
Adjust the plan when your circumstances change.

quiz.prompt: What does a budget do?
options: Plans how available money is used
quiz.explanation: A budget connects resources and priorities.

quiz.prompt: You have $200 and plan $150 of necessities; what remains?
quiz.explanation: Subtract necessities from available money.

lessons.title: Choosing an Account
lessons.objective: Explain choosing an account and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Checking supports frequent payments, while savings can hold money for later.
Compare fees, minimum balances, access, and conditions.
A debit card uses account funds rather than providing extra income.
Review statements and unfamiliar activity.

quiz.prompt: Which detail matters when choosing checking?
quiz.explanation: Conditions affect cost and usability.

quiz.prompt: A $5 monthly fee costs how much in 12 months?
quiz.explanation: Multiply the monthly fee by 12.

lessons.title: Gross Is Not Take-Home
lessons.objective: Explain gross is not take-home and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Gross pay is earnings before deductions.
Net pay is what remains after deductions.
Use net pay when planning spendable money.
Review the pay statement and check hours or agreed compensation.

quiz.prompt: Which amount is take-home pay?
quiz.explanation: Net pay reflects deductions.

quiz.prompt: A fictional payment is $200 gross with $20 deductions; net is what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the example deductions; this is not a universal tax rate.

lessons.title: Beyond the Sticker Price
lessons.objective: Explain beyond the sticker price and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: An advertised price may exclude required costs.
Include fees, maintenance, supplies, and practical restrictions.
Compare options that meet the same need.
The cheapest option is useful only if it actually works for you.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in a purchase comparison?
quiz.explanation: Required costs change the real total.

quiz.prompt: A $50 item needs a $10 required accessory; total is what?
quiz.explanation: Add the necessary accessory cost.

lessons.title: Priorities Can Differ
lessons.objective: Explain priorities can differ and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Needs support necessary living and responsibilities.
Wants can provide enjoyment and still deserve a place in a budget.
Circumstances change which expenses are urgent.
Compare a purchase with your own obligations rather than someone else's lifestyle.

quiz.prompt: Should everyone have exactly the same spending priorities?
quiz.explanation: Needs and priorities depend on circumstances.

quiz.prompt: A $30 optional purchase leaves what from $80?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the purchase from available money.

lessons.title: The Repeating Charge
lessons.objective: Explain the repeating charge and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Subscriptions repeat under their terms until canceled.
A trial can turn into a paid renewal.
Compare ongoing cost with actual use and check cancellation rules.
Put renewal dates in a place you will review.

quiz.prompt: What should you check before a trial?
quiz.explanation: The future charge is part of the offer.

quiz.prompt: $8 monthly for three months totals what?
quiz.explanation: Multiply 8 by 3.

lessons.title: A Cushion for Surprises
lessons.objective: Explain a cushion for surprises and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: An emergency fund holds accessible money for unplanned necessary expenses.
Using it appropriately is part of its purpose.
Compare repairs, replacements, and support before spending.
Rebuild the cushion at a pace that fits your situation.

quiz.prompt: Which fits an emergency fund?
quiz.explanation: The fund is for unplanned necessary costs.

quiz.prompt: Using $40 from $100 saved leaves what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the expense from savings.

lessons.title: Saving for a Known Cost
lessons.objective: Explain saving for a known cost and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A sinking fund sets money aside for a predictable expense.
An emergency fund serves a different purpose.
Goal labels organize existing money rather than creating more.
Change the goal when costs or priorities change.

quiz.prompt: Which is a sinking-fund goal?
quiz.explanation: A planned expense can be saved for ahead of time.

quiz.prompt: A $300 target with $120 already saved has what gap?
quiz.explanation: Subtract progress from the target.

lessons.title: Time Has a Cost Too
lessons.objective: Explain time has a cost too and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Earning more can require more time or effort.
Compare extra income with obligations, rest, and other goals.
Paying for convenience can be reasonable when the saved time matters.
Neither working more nor spending less is automatically the best choice.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in an extra-work decision?
quiz.explanation: Time and workload affect the choice.

quiz.prompt: A $50 task requires $15 travel; what remains before other costs?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the required travel expense.

lessons.title: Borrowing Is Not Income
lessons.objective: Explain borrowing is not income and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Credit gives access to borrowed money under repayment terms.
A credit limit is not savings or income.
Purchases create obligations even if no cash leaves checking immediately.
Read the terms before deciding whether borrowing fits the need.

quiz.prompt: What is a credit limit?
options: An amount available to borrow under terms
quiz.explanation: Borrowed money must be repaid.

quiz.prompt: An $80 balance minus a $20 principal payment leaves what before new charges?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the payment from the balance.

lessons.title: Reports and Scores
lessons.objective: Explain reports and scores and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A credit report records information about borrowing history.
A credit score summarizes selected report information using a scoring model.
Review reports for accuracy and dispute errors through legitimate channels.
No single action guarantees a particular score change.

quiz.prompt: Are a report and a score identical?
quiz.explanation: A report contains information; a score summarizes selected information.

quiz.prompt: What should you do about an unfamiliar account?
options: Pay a stranger to erase it immediately
quiz.explanation: Use official channels to investigate.

lessons.title: The Minimum Is Not the Total
lessons.objective: Explain the minimum is not the total and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A minimum payment is the required minimum for a statement, not full repayment.
Paying only it leaves a balance and may lead to interest.
Purchase grace periods depend on the agreement and balance status.
When applicable, full statement payment by the due date can avoid purchase interest.

quiz.prompt: Does paying the minimum erase all debt?
quiz.explanation: An unpaid balance remains.

quiz.prompt: A $100 statement minus $25 paid leaves what before interest?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the payment; interest is separate.

lessons.title: Read the Whole Loan
lessons.objective: Explain read the whole loan and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A loan has principal, costs, a term, and repayment conditions.
Compare total repayment rather than the smallest advertised payment.
Collateral and missed-payment consequences matter too.
Borrowing can solve a need while reducing future flexibility.

quiz.prompt: What should a loan comparison include?
quiz.explanation: The whole commitment affects cost and risk.

quiz.prompt: Four payments of $30 total what?
quiz.explanation: Multiply the payment by four.

lessons.title: Rates, Fees, and Total Cost
lessons.objective: Explain rates, fees, and total cost and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: APR is a borrowing-cost measure expressed annually and can include certain fees under applicable rules.
Compare equivalent offers and read what is included.
A lower payment can still mean a longer and more expensive loan.
Calculate total repayment for the actual term.

quiz.prompt: Can a smaller monthly payment mean higher total cost?
quiz.explanation: A longer repayment term can increase total cost.

quiz.prompt: Twelve payments of $20 total what?
quiz.explanation: Multiply 12 by 20 before adding separately disclosed costs.

lessons.title: Making a Repayment Plan
lessons.objective: Explain making a repayment plan and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: List balances, rates, and required payments before prioritizing debt.
Avalanche targets higher-rate debt first, while snowball targets smaller balances first.
Keep necessary payments and living costs in the plan.
Seek legitimate help when the schedule is not affordable.

quiz.prompt: Which strategy prioritizes higher interest rates?
quiz.explanation: Avalanche targets the highest-rate balance first.

quiz.prompt: A $200 balance with $50 of principal repaid becomes what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the principal repayment.

lessons.title: Pause and Verify
lessons.objective: Explain pause and verify and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Scams often use urgency, secrecy, or impersonation.
Verify requests through an independent trusted channel.
Do not share passwords or verification codes with callers or messages.
A familiar name does not prove a request is genuine.

quiz.prompt: How should you verify a suspicious request?
quiz.explanation: An independent route avoids trusting the sender.

quiz.prompt: Does a message using your name prove it is genuine?
quiz.explanation: Personal details can be copied.

lessons.title: Protecting Account Access
lessons.objective: Explain protecting account access and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Use strong unique passwords and available multifactor authentication.
Keep recovery information and verification codes private.
Review unfamiliar activity through official channels.
Security habits reduce risk without making fraud impossible.

quiz.prompt: Should a caller receive your login code?
options: Yes if they know your name
quiz.explanation: Codes protect account access.

quiz.prompt: What is a useful security habit?
quiz.explanation: Reviewing activity can reveal problems.

lessons.title: Withholding and the Final Bill
lessons.objective: Explain withholding and the final bill and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Withholding pays toward a possible tax liability during the year.
A return reconciles applicable tax with payments and other relevant information.
A refund is not guaranteed extra earnings.
Keep records and use reliable help for your situation.

quiz.prompt: Does withholding always equal final tax liability?
quiz.explanation: The final result depends on the full applicable information.

quiz.prompt: In a simplified example, $120 paid toward a $100 bill leaves what difference?
quiz.explanation: The example has paid $20 more than that bill.

lessons.title: Comparing an Offer
lessons.objective: Explain comparing an offer and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Compensation includes more than a headline salary.
Compare expected take-home pay, costs, hours, benefits, and reliability.
Ask for clear written terms and prepare questions.
A larger number is not automatically a better fit.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in comparing offers?
quiz.explanation: The whole arrangement determines its value.

quiz.prompt: $200 extra take-home with $80 added travel leaves what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the additional required cost.

lessons.title: Benefits Are Part of Compensation
lessons.objective: Explain benefits are part of compensation and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Benefits can include insurance, paid leave, and retirement contributions.
Eligibility, employee costs, and restrictions vary.
Compare the benefits you can actually use with cash compensation.
Read the plan rather than assuming every employer offers the same terms.

quiz.prompt: What should you check in a benefit?
quiz.explanation: The terms determine actual usefulness.

quiz.prompt: A benefit costs you $20 each of four pay periods; total is what?
quiz.explanation: Multiply the employee cost by four.

lessons.title: What Coverage Protects
lessons.objective: Explain what coverage protects and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Insurance covers specified risks under policy terms.
Premiums pay for coverage, while limits and exclusions define its boundaries.
A deductible may be your share of a covered loss.
Compare the policy with the risk and what you could afford to lose.

quiz.prompt: Does a policy cover every possible loss?
quiz.explanation: Coverage depends on the actual terms.

quiz.prompt: A simplified covered $300 loss with a $100 deductible leaves insurer payment of what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the deductible, assuming sufficient applicable coverage.

lessons.title: Choosing a Deductible
lessons.objective: Explain choosing a deductible and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A deductible affects what you may pay on a covered claim.
A lower premium may come with a higher deductible or other differences.
Compare equivalent coverage and your available reserves.
A cheap premium is not the full risk cost.

quiz.prompt: What should you compare alongside premium?
options: Only the color of the document
quiz.explanation: Lower price can shift more risk to you.

quiz.prompt: A deductible rises from $100 to $250; increase is what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the old deductible from the new one.

lessons.title: Renting and Buying
lessons.objective: Explain renting and buying and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Housing costs include more than rent or a mortgage payment.
Include taxes, insurance, utilities, upkeep, fees, and moving costs where applicable.
Buying and renting offer different commitments and flexibility.
Compare the full cost with your expected time horizon.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in housing affordability?
quiz.explanation: Other necessary housing expenses matter.

quiz.prompt: $500 rent plus $80 utilities totals what?
quiz.explanation: Add the required costs.

lessons.title: Before You Sign
lessons.objective: Explain before you sign and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A lease or service contract creates obligations under its terms.
Review duration, payments, deposits, exit rules, and responsibility for damage.
Ask for clarification before committing.
A refundable deposit still ties up accessible money.

quiz.prompt: Does refundable mean a deposit remains spendable while held?
quiz.explanation: Money held as a deposit is not currently available to spend.

quiz.prompt: $700 upfront rent plus a $300 deposit requires what cash?
quiz.explanation: Add both upfront cash requirements; they may have different accounting treatment.

lessons.title: Review Before the Next Step
lessons.objective: Explain review before the next step and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Review available money, investments, debts, and upcoming commitments together.
Compare results with your original plan and circumstances.
Separate transfers from income and investment value changes from cash.
Choose an achievable next step rather than a perfect-looking balance.

quiz.prompt: What should a review include?
quiz.explanation: Different measures reveal different parts of the situation.

quiz.prompt: $100 checking plus $150 savings equals what before other assets and debts?
quiz.explanation: Add the accounts without double counting transfers.

lessons.title: Timing Can Change the Answer
lessons.objective: Explain timing can change the answer and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Cash flow tracks when money arrives and leaves.
A profitable month can still have a shortage before payment arrives.
Put income and bill dates on the same calendar.
A delayed payment is not cash you can already spend.

quiz.prompt: Can a positive monthly total hide a temporary shortage?
quiz.explanation: Payment timing can leave a gap.

quiz.prompt: $100 available with an $80 bill before payday leaves what?
quiz.explanation: Only current available money covers that bill.

lessons.title: What Money Can Buy
lessons.objective: Explain what money can buy and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Inflation is a rise in the general price level.
Personal expenses can change differently from the overall measure.
If relevant prices rise while your money stays fixed, purchasing power falls.
Review actual costs instead of assuming pay rises at the same rate.

quiz.prompt: What happens when prices rise but available money does not?
quiz.explanation: The same money buys less of the affected goods.

quiz.prompt: A $10 price rises to $11; percentage rise is what?
quiz.explanation: A $1 rise is one tenth of $10.

lessons.title: Soon or Later?
lessons.objective: Explain soon or later? and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Savings and investments serve different goals.
Volatile assets can fall when money is needed soon.
A longer horizon may allow more time for fluctuations but does not guarantee profit.
Match risk with when and why you need the money.

quiz.prompt: Which money is poorly suited to volatile stocks?
quiz.explanation: Near-term obligations need reliable access and value.

quiz.prompt: Can an investment lose value?
quiz.explanation: Investment results are uncertain.

lessons.title: Willing Versus Able
lessons.objective: Explain willing versus able and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Risk tolerance is how comfortable you feel with uncertainty.
Risk capacity is how much loss your finances can withstand.
They can differ even for the same person.
Consider goals, obligations, support, and time horizon before taking risk.

quiz.prompt: Does feeling comfortable prove you can afford a loss?
quiz.explanation: Willingness and financial capacity are different.

quiz.prompt: A $100 holding falls 20 percent; value becomes what?
quiz.explanation: A 20 percent loss is $20.

lessons.title: Growth on Earlier Growth
lessons.objective: Explain growth on earlier growth and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Compounding includes returns on earlier returns.
Time, contributions, costs, and the actual sequence of returns affect outcomes.
Real investments do not grow at a fixed guaranteed rate.
A calculator illustrates assumptions rather than predicting your future.

quiz.prompt: Does a fixed-rate investment illustration guarantee that result?
quiz.explanation: The illustration depends on assumptions.

quiz.prompt: Hypothetically, $100 growing 10 percent twice becomes what?
quiz.explanation: 100 becomes 110, then 121.

lessons.title: Owning a Share
lessons.objective: Explain owning a share and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A stock represents ownership in a company.
Prices change as buyers and sellers reassess the business and expectations.
Some companies pay dividends, but payments can change or stop.
One company exposes you to company-specific risk.

quiz.prompt: What does a share represent?
quiz.explanation: Common shares are an ownership interest.

quiz.prompt: A share moves from $20 to $15; change is what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the original price from the new price.

lessons.title: Look at Total Return
lessons.objective: Explain look at total return and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A dividend distributes value to holders under the investment's terms.
It can change or stop.
Total return includes distributions and market value changes.
A large yield alone does not establish safety or suitability.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in total return?
quiz.explanation: Both components matter.

quiz.prompt: A holding loses $5 in value and pays $2; combined change is what?
quiz.explanation: Add negative 5 and positive 2 before costs.

lessons.title: Lending Through a Bond
lessons.objective: Explain lending through a bond and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A bond is a debt investment with specified obligations.
Interest, maturity, default risk, and price changes all matter.
Selling before maturity can produce a loss or gain.
A bond fund differs from holding one bond to maturity.

quiz.prompt: A bond generally represents what?
quiz.explanation: Bonds are debt investments.

quiz.prompt: $4 annual interest on $100 principal is what percentage?
quiz.explanation: Divide 4 by 100; this is only a sample.

lessons.title: What a Fund Holds
lessons.objective: Explain what a fund holds and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A fund pools money to hold investments.
ETFs and mutual funds are structures, while indexing describes a strategy.
Check holdings, purpose, risk, and costs.
A narrow fund can remain concentrated despite owning several assets.

quiz.prompt: Does every ETF provide broad diversification?
quiz.explanation: The actual holdings determine concentration.

quiz.prompt: What does an index strategy aim to do?
quiz.explanation: Tracking does not guarantee a return.

lessons.title: Spreading Exposure
lessons.objective: Explain spreading exposure and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Diversification spreads exposure among different investments.
It can reduce some risks without preventing all losses.
Several funds can overlap heavily.
Look through the labels to understand the underlying holdings.

quiz.prompt: Can diversified investments still lose value?
quiz.explanation: Diversification is not a guarantee against loss.

quiz.prompt: Two funds both concentrated in the same sector may have what issue?
quiz.explanation: Different labels can hide similar exposure.

lessons.title: The Account and the Investment
lessons.objective: Explain the account and the investment and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A brokerage account holds cash and investments.
Funding it does not automatically buy a holding.
Cash accounts use available funds while margin involves borrowing and additional risk.
Brokerage protection does not cover ordinary market losses.

quiz.prompt: Is a brokerage account itself a stock?
quiz.explanation: The account is a container.

quiz.prompt: What does margin add?
quiz.explanation: Borrowing can magnify losses.

lessons.title: Market or Limit?
lessons.objective: Explain market or limit? and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A market order prioritizes execution without guaranteeing the displayed price.
A limit order sets a price condition and may not fill.
Understand the order before confirming.
An unfilled order creates no holding.

quiz.prompt: Which order specifies a price condition?
quiz.explanation: A limit controls the acceptable buy or sell price.

quiz.prompt: Can a limit order remain unfilled?
quiz.explanation: The market may not meet its condition.

lessons.title: Small Fees Add Up
lessons.objective: Explain small fees add up and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Fees reduce what an investor retains.
Percentage and fixed charges can affect small and large accounts differently.
Compare equivalent services and holdings.
Lower cost does not remove market risk.

quiz.prompt: What do fees do to retained returns?
quiz.explanation: Fees are costs.

quiz.prompt: One percent of $1,000 is what?
quiz.explanation: One percent is one part in one hundred.

lessons.title: Check the Source
lessons.objective: Explain check the source and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A confident claim is not proof.
Review evidence, uncertainty, compensation, and conflicts of interest.
Compare with independent reliable sources.
Another person's goals may differ from yours.

quiz.prompt: Why check a promoter's compensation?
quiz.explanation: Incentives can influence a claim.

quiz.prompt: Does follower count prove suitability?
quiz.explanation: Popularity is not evidence of suitability.

lessons.title: A Price Move Is Not a Plan
lessons.objective: Explain a price move is not a plan and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A recent price change does not establish what comes next.
Revisit your goal, time horizon, and need for cash before trading.
Holding and selling both involve trade-offs.
No reasonable decision guarantees a favorable outcome.

quiz.prompt: Does a recent gain guarantee another?
quiz.explanation: Past movements do not determine future results.

quiz.prompt: A $20 holding is worth $18; current change is what?
quiz.explanation: Compare current value with the original value.

lessons.title: Accounts for a Future Goal
lessons.objective: Explain accounts for a future goal and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Retirement planning prepares for spending beyond current earning years.
Account types have eligibility, tax, contribution, and withdrawal rules.
An account may hold investments rather than being an investment itself.
Verify applicable rules and choose holdings deliberately.

quiz.prompt: Is a retirement account identical to a particular fund?
quiz.explanation: The account and holdings are different.

quiz.prompt: Does contributing cash automatically specify how it is invested?
quiz.explanation: Account funding and investment selection can be separate steps.

lessons.title: Understand the Match
lessons.objective: Explain understand the match and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: An employer may add retirement contributions under a plan formula.
Eligibility, contribution requirements, and vesting vary.
Read the actual plan before counting benefits.
A match does not remove investment risk or every other financial priority.

quiz.prompt: What must you check before counting a match?
quiz.explanation: The plan defines the contribution.

quiz.prompt: A fictional plan matches half of a qualifying $100 contribution; match is what?
quiz.explanation: Half of 100 is 50.

lessons.title: Tax Timing in Retirement Accounts
lessons.objective: Explain tax timing in retirement accounts and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Traditional and Roth arrangements differ in tax treatment.
Eligibility and qualified withdrawal rules matter.
Which is suitable depends on circumstances and future uncertainty.
Verify current rules rather than assuming one always wins.

quiz.prompt: Is one tax treatment best for everyone?
quiz.explanation: Circumstances and applicable rules differ.

quiz.prompt: What should you verify before using an account?
quiz.explanation: Account rules affect the decision.

lessons.title: A Mix That Fits the Goal
lessons.objective: Explain a mix that fits the goal and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Asset allocation is how a portfolio is divided among asset types.
Match the mix to goals, time horizon, and ability to absorb losses.
Check concentration and overlap.
A suitable mix still has uncertain returns.

quiz.prompt: What should guide allocation?
quiz.explanation: The portfolio should fit the owner's situation.

quiz.prompt: A $100 portfolio with $60 stock exposure has what stock share?
quiz.explanation: 60 divided by 100 is 60 percent.

lessons.title: Returning to Your Intended Mix
lessons.objective: Explain returning to your intended mix and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Price changes can move a portfolio away from its intended allocation.
Rebalancing adjusts the mix toward a chosen plan.
Consider costs, taxes, and new contributions.
It is different from constantly chasing recent winners.

quiz.prompt: What is rebalancing intended to do?
quiz.explanation: It manages allocation rather than predicting prices.

quiz.prompt: A $100 portfolio has $70 stocks but a $60 target; excess is what?
quiz.explanation: Compare current stock value with the target.

lessons.title: When Income Changes
lessons.objective: Explain when income changes and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Income can vary or stop while commitments continue.
Plan using reliable resources and realistic scenarios.
Accessible reserves and flexible costs can help bridge gaps.
A high earning period is not a guarantee of future income.

quiz.prompt: Does a strong month guarantee the next?
quiz.explanation: Income can change under actual terms and circumstances.

quiz.prompt: A $300 reserve covering $100 of expenses each month lasts how long without other changes?
quiz.explanation: Divide reserves by monthly expenses.

lessons.title: Read What You Are Promising
lessons.objective: Explain read what you are promising and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Contracts define payments, duties, timing, and other conditions.
A headline amount may depend on milestones or other requirements.
Review exit rules and obligations before agreeing.
Seek qualified help for terms you do not understand.

quiz.prompt: Does a headline contract amount explain all conditions?
quiz.explanation: Terms determine what must happen and when.

quiz.prompt: A $1,000 contract pays $400 first; unpaid remainder is what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the initial payment from the total.

lessons.title: Advice Has Terms Too
lessons.objective: Explain advice has terms too and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Financial professionals have different roles and compensation.
Check registration, background, services, fees, and conflicts through appropriate independent sources.
A professional cannot guarantee market outcomes.
Understand what you are paying for before agreeing.

quiz.prompt: What should you check about an adviser?
quiz.explanation: Independent checks and terms matter.

quiz.prompt: A hypothetical 1 percent fee on $10,000 is what for that calculation?
quiz.explanation: Multiply 10000 by 0.01; actual billing terms may differ.

lessons.title: Revenue Is Not Profit
lessons.objective: Explain revenue is not profit and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Revenue is money earned from sales before expenses.
Profit subtracts relevant costs under the accounting method used.
Cash available can differ from either figure because of timing.
Keep business records that distinguish all three.

quiz.prompt: Is revenue automatically profit?
quiz.explanation: Costs must be considered.

quiz.prompt: $500 revenue minus $350 costs leaves what before other expenses and taxes?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the stated costs.

lessons.title: Costs That Move Differently
lessons.objective: Explain costs that move differently and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Fixed costs do not change directly with each extra unit within a relevant range.
Variable costs change with activity.
Both belong in a realistic budget.
A cost can behave differently at another scale or under another contract.

quiz.prompt: Which is typically variable in a simple production example?
quiz.explanation: Materials increase as more items are produced.

quiz.prompt: $5 materials for each of 10 items totals what?
quiz.explanation: Multiply unit cost by quantity.

lessons.title: Covering the Costs
lessons.objective: Explain covering the costs and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Break-even is where revenue covers the stated costs.
Contribution per unit is price minus variable cost.
Divide relevant fixed costs by positive contribution to estimate required units.
Check the assumptions before treating the result as a forecast.

quiz.prompt: What is contribution per unit?
quiz.explanation: Contribution helps cover fixed costs.

quiz.prompt: $100 fixed cost and $10 contribution per item require how many items to break even?
quiz.explanation: Divide 100 by 10.

lessons.title: A Price That Can Work
lessons.objective: Explain a price that can work and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Pricing should account for costs, customer value, and realistic demand.
Discounting may increase sales without improving profit.
Compare the contribution and workload of an offer.
A higher price also does not guarantee customers will buy.

quiz.prompt: Can a discount increase sales while reducing profit?
quiz.explanation: More volume may not cover lower contribution.

quiz.prompt: Price $50 minus variable cost $30 gives what contribution?
quiz.explanation: Subtract variable cost from price.

lessons.title: An Invoice Is Not Cash
lessons.objective: Explain an invoice is not cash and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Accounts receivable are amounts customers owe.
They are not already available bank funds.
Payment timing, clear terms, and follow-up affect cash flow.
Do not spend an expected receipt as though it has cleared.

quiz.prompt: Is an unpaid invoice spendable bank cash?
quiz.explanation: It is a claim to payment, not cleared cash.

quiz.prompt: $600 invoiced with $200 collected leaves what receivable?
quiz.explanation: Subtract collected money from the invoice.

lessons.title: Funding the Gap
lessons.objective: Explain funding the gap and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Operations may require cash before a customer pays.
Forecast the gap between receipts and required payments.
A large contract can create pressure despite expected profit.
Compare deposits, phased work, reserves, and financing under clear terms.

quiz.prompt: Can a profitable contract cause a cash shortage?
quiz.explanation: Costs can arrive before receipts.

quiz.prompt: $500 upfront costs with $300 available leaves what gap?
quiz.explanation: Subtract available cash from required cost.

lessons.title: Borrowing or Sharing Ownership
lessons.objective: Explain borrowing or sharing ownership and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Debt creates repayment obligations under terms.
Equity gives an ownership interest and can change control and future profit shares.
Compare costs, risk, flexibility, and expectations.
Neither source is free money.

quiz.prompt: What does equity financing exchange?
quiz.explanation: Investors receive an interest under agreed terms.

quiz.prompt: Does borrowing ordinarily require repayment under terms?
quiz.explanation: Debt creates obligations independent of hoped-for success.

lessons.title: A Smaller Slice of a Changed Pie
lessons.objective: Explain a smaller slice of a changed pie and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Issuing ownership interests can reduce an existing owner's percentage.
The business may gain resources in exchange.
Consider valuation, control, and agreement terms.
A smaller percentage is not automatically a worse outcome.

quiz.prompt: What is ownership dilution?
options: A reduction in an existing percentage interest
quiz.explanation: New ownership can change relative shares.

quiz.prompt: If 100 old shares remain and 100 new shares are issued, the old shares represent what of 200 total?
quiz.explanation: 100 divided by 200 equals half.

lessons.title: Business Money and Personal Money
lessons.objective: Explain business money and personal money and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Business and personal funds serve different responsibilities.
Record transfers between them clearly.
An owner draw is not a new customer sale.
A business account balance is not automatically money safe to spend personally.

quiz.prompt: Is an owner draw a new sale?
quiz.explanation: It transfers existing funds.

quiz.prompt: $500 business cash with a $100 draw leaves what business cash before other changes?
quiz.explanation: The personal account receives the same transfer; combined cash is unchanged.

lessons.title: Setting Aside Is Not Paying Tax
lessons.objective: Explain setting aside is not paying tax and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Income without sufficient withholding can create a future tax obligation.
Keep records and estimate using qualified help and applicable rules.
A reserve is money set aside, not a tax payment or a deduction by itself.
Review the estimate when income changes.

quiz.prompt: Does moving money to a reserve mean tax is paid?
quiz.explanation: A reserve remains an asset until an actual payment.

quiz.prompt: Moving $40 from $200 into a reserve leaves unrestricted cash of what?
quiz.explanation: The combined cash remains $200.

lessons.title: What Is Owned and Owed
lessons.objective: Explain what is owned and owed and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A balance sheet summarizes assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time.
Cash is only one asset.
Loans and unpaid obligations belong among liabilities.
Profit over a period is a different measure.

quiz.prompt: Does a balance sheet describe only cash?
quiz.explanation: It includes other assets and liabilities.

quiz.prompt: $1,000 assets minus $600 liabilities gives what equity?
quiz.explanation: Subtract liabilities from assets.

lessons.title: What Matters From Here
lessons.objective: Explain what matters from here and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A sunk cost has already been incurred and cannot be recovered by the next decision.
It does not by itself justify more spending.
Compare future costs, benefits, and alternatives.
Changing direction can be reasonable when information changes.

quiz.prompt: Should past spending alone force another purchase?
quiz.explanation: The next decision depends on future consequences.

quiz.prompt: A $20 research trip does not provide how much of a new $100 payment?
quiz.explanation: The earlier cost is not available money.

lessons.title: Property Is an Investment Too
lessons.objective: Explain property is an investment too and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Property can have income, costs, debt, and uncertain value.
Maintenance, vacancies, fees, taxes, and insurance affect results.
Selling can take time and cost money.
A rental headline is not guaranteed profit or ready cash.

quiz.prompt: Is advertised rent the same as profit?
quiz.explanation: Expenses and financing must be considered.

quiz.prompt: $1,000 rent minus $700 stated costs leaves what before other items?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the stated costs.

lessons.title: Giving With a Plan
lessons.objective: Explain giving with a plan and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Giving can reflect personal values and support others.
Verify the recipient and any conditions.
Choose an amount that fits obligations and resources.
Do not assume every donation creates a tax benefit.

quiz.prompt: What should you verify before donating?
options: The recipient and use of funds
quiz.explanation: Check independently that the recipient is legitimate.

quiz.prompt: A $15 gift from $60 leaves what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the gift.

lessons.title: Helping Without Overpromising
lessons.objective: Explain helping without overpromising and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Support can involve money, time, or practical help.
Check your own commitments before promising money.
Clarify whether money is a gift or loan.
Declining a payment does not mean you cannot care about someone.

quiz.prompt: Must helpful support always involve money?
quiz.explanation: Time and practical help can matter.

quiz.prompt: A $25 gift from $100 leaves what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the gift.

lessons.title: Accessible When Needed
lessons.objective: Explain accessible when needed and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Liquidity describes how readily an asset can be turned into usable money.
Selling may take time or expose you to a loss.
A valuable asset is not always suitable for an imminent bill.
Match accessible resources with payment timing.

quiz.prompt: Does a valuable asset always solve a bill due today?
quiz.explanation: Access and timing matter.

quiz.prompt: $80 accessible cash against a $100 bill leaves what gap?
quiz.explanation: Subtract accessible money from the bill.

lessons.title: The Too-Good Promise
lessons.objective: Explain the too-good promise and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: High returns without risk are a warning sign.
Check the investment and promoter independently.
Secrecy, urgency, and recruitment pressure deserve scrutiny.
Choosing not to send money preserves options while you investigate.

quiz.prompt: Which is a warning sign?
options: Guaranteed high return with no risk
quiz.explanation: The promise hides or denies risk.

quiz.prompt: Does a testimonial establish that returns are guaranteed?
quiz.explanation: A testimonial is not a guarantee or independent verification.

lessons.title: Measuring the Whole Result
lessons.objective: Explain measuring the whole result and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Performance includes income and value changes over a stated period.
Compare costs and relevant risk as well as returns.
Deposits are not investment gains.
Distinguish realized results from changes in holdings not sold.

quiz.prompt: Is a new contribution an investment return?
quiz.explanation: It is money added by the owner.

quiz.prompt: A $100 holding plus a $20 contribution ends at $125; gain before other adjustments is what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the starting amount and added contribution.

lessons.title: Keeping Important Details Current
lessons.objective: Explain keeping important details current and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Some accounts and policies use beneficiary designations.
Review them when circumstances change.
Estate documents and account rules can interact in ways requiring qualified help.
A will alone does not explain every account's treatment.

quiz.prompt: What can a beneficiary review help check?
options: Who is designated under applicable terms
quiz.explanation: Designations affect specified account or policy arrangements.

quiz.prompt: Should important changes prompt a review?
quiz.explanation: Relevant life changes can make old instructions unsuitable.

lessons.title: A Clear Interest Example
lessons.objective: Explain a clear interest example and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Simple interest uses principal, rate, and time under stated assumptions.
Real agreements may use different calculation methods or include fees.
Read the applicable formula and schedule.
An illustration is not a quote for an actual product.

quiz.prompt: What inputs does simple interest use?
quiz.explanation: The calculation requires all three inputs.

quiz.prompt: $100 at 5 percent simple annual interest for one year produces what interest?
quiz.explanation: Multiply 100 by 0.05 by 1.

lessons.title: Know What Is Protected
lessons.objective: Explain know what is protected and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: Eligible bank or credit-union deposits can have government-backed insurance subject to coverage rules.
Check the institution, ownership category, and applicable limits.
Stocks and funds are not insured deposits merely because an app offers them.
Brokerage protection does not insure ordinary market losses.

quiz.prompt: Is a stock an insured bank deposit?
quiz.explanation: Product type matters.

quiz.prompt: What should you verify about deposit protection?
quiz.explanation: Coverage depends on the institution and arrangement.

lessons.title: A Sustainable Next Chapter
lessons.objective: Explain a sustainable next chapter and apply the concept to a financial comparison.
sentences: A financial review should test what happens if income changes or a cost arrives early.
Check accessible reserves, commitments, protection, and concentrated risks.
A plan can be revised without erasing what you learned.
Financial progress should support a sustainable life.

quiz.prompt: What makes a useful final plan?
quiz.explanation: A workable plan leaves room for uncertainty.

quiz.prompt: Two months of $100 necessities require what before other costs?
quiz.explanation: Multiply the monthly cost by two.

lessons.title: A Scholarship Application
lessons.objective: Distinguish grants and scholarships from loans.
sentences: Scholarships and grants generally do not require repayment when their conditions are met.
Loans must be repaid under their terms.
Check eligibility, deadlines, and renewal requirements before relying on an award.
Applying does not guarantee receiving money.

quiz.prompt: Which normally needs repayment?
quiz.explanation: Loans are borrowed funds.
options: An eligible scholarship used under its conditions
A grant used under its conditions

quiz.prompt: Is an application the same as a confirmed award?
quiz.explanation: Budget with confirmed resources rather than hoped-for awards.

lessons.title: Selling What You No Longer Use
lessons.objective: Account for selling costs and safe payment.
sentences: Selling an unused item can free money without adding work hours.
Sale proceeds are not the same as profit from a business.
Account for fees and check that payment is genuine.
Use safe exchange methods rather than trusting a payment screenshot.

quiz.prompt: What should you verify before handing over an item?
quiz.explanation: Screenshots can be misleading.

quiz.prompt: A sale is $30 with a $5 fee; what do you receive?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the fee from the sale proceeds.

lessons.title: Before the First Final
lessons.objective: Plan time alongside financial commitments.
sentences: A useful plan accounts for deadlines as well as spending.
Preparation can reduce last-minute pressure.
Paid help is not automatically better than free support.
Choose resources that fit the task and your schedule.

quiz.prompt: What can a plan include besides money?
quiz.explanation: Time planning supports realistic commitments.

quiz.prompt: You need four study hours and finish one; how many remain?
quiz.explanation: Subtract completed time from the plan.

lessons.title: What Your Aid Actually Covers
lessons.objective: Distinguish confirmed grants, loans, and unmet costs.
sentences: An aid offer can combine grants, scholarships, work-study, and loans.
Loans create repayment obligations, while other awards have their own conditions.
Compare confirmed aid with the full education cost.
Contact the aid office when an item or condition is unclear.

quiz.prompt: Which aid is borrowed money?
quiz.explanation: A loan creates a repayment obligation.

quiz.prompt: Costs are $1,000 and confirmed grant aid is $700; what remains before other funding?
quiz.explanation: Subtract confirmed aid from costs.

lessons.title: Learning a Skill for Work
lessons.objective: Compare training cost with uncertain future value.
sentences: Training can build useful skills but does not guarantee a job.
Compare price, quality, time, and relevance.
Free resources may teach the same skill as a paid course.
Judge a course by what it helps you do rather than a promised salary.

quiz.prompt: Does paying for a course guarantee higher income?
quiz.explanation: Training outcomes remain uncertain.
options: Only if the advertisement says so

quiz.prompt: A $40 course and $10 materials total what?
quiz.explanation: Include required materials.

lessons.title: Next Year's Address
lessons.objective: Compare full housing costs and commitments.
sentences: Housing cost includes more than advertised rent.
Utilities, deposits, transport, furniture, and lease terms can change affordability.
A refundable deposit ties up money even when it is not an expense.
Compare the full arrangement before signing.

quiz.prompt: What should you add to advertised rent?
quiz.explanation: The full cost determines affordability.
options: Required utilities and other housing costs

quiz.prompt: Rent is $500 and utilities $80; monthly cost is what?
quiz.explanation: Add rent and utilities.

lessons.title: The Roommate Agreement
lessons.objective: Clarify responsibilities before sharing costs.
sentences: Shared expenses need clear agreements.
Discuss who pays, when money is due, and how changes will be handled.
A friendly promise is not a substitute for understanding a lease.
Agreeing early can prevent confusion without guaranteeing there will never be conflict.

quiz.prompt: What should roommates clarify?
quiz.explanation: Clear responsibilities reduce misunderstandings.

quiz.prompt: A shared $60 item split equally between two people costs each what?
quiz.explanation: Divide by two.

lessons.title: A Side-Gig Offer
lessons.objective: Distinguish revenue from expenses and uncertain tax obligations.
sentences: Gig income may arrive without automatic tax withholding.
Track payments and related expenses.
Revenue is the amount received before subtracting costs.
Set aside records and get reliable help with applicable taxes.

quiz.prompt: A client payment before costs is what?
quiz.explanation: Costs still need to be considered.

quiz.prompt: A $50 payment needs $10 materials; what remains before taxes?
quiz.explanation: Subtract materials; tax treatment is a separate issue.

lessons.title: Choose Your Summer
lessons.objective: Choose a sustainable income and time arrangement.
sentences: A workable plan balances income with costs and commitments.
Higher earnings can require more time or effort.
Compare realistic take-home pay and necessary expenses.
Your choice can be revised when circumstances change.

quiz.prompt: What should guide a summer work choice?
quiz.explanation: The best fit depends on several priorities.

quiz.prompt: A $180 fortnightly take-home payment minus $140 necessities leaves what?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the necessities from take-home pay.

lessons.title: A Plan Longer Than One Summer
lessons.objective: Connect diversification, compounding, and retirement account concepts.
sentences: Long-term investing combines contributions, time, costs, and uncertain returns.
Compound growth includes returns on earlier returns, but actual investment results fluctuate.
Retirement accounts have eligibility and tax rules and can hold investments rather than being investments themselves.
Build a plan around goals and diversified exposure instead of promised growth.

quiz.prompt: Is a retirement account itself the same as an ETF?
quiz.explanation: An account is a container with rules, not a particular holding.
options: No; the account may hold investments

quiz.prompt: In a purely hypothetical two-year example, $100 grows 10 percent each year; value becomes what?
quiz.explanation: 100 becomes 110, then 110 times 1.10 is 121; real returns are not fixed.

sources.title: FDIC Money Smart for Young Adults
